lessons.title: Why Hard Work Alone Leaves You Broke
lessons.key_idea: Bansir works hard for years and still has nothing, which shows that wealth comes from understanding the laws of money, not from labor or luck alone.

lessons.title: A Part of All You Earn
lessons.key_idea: Arkad's first secret is to pay yourself first by keeping at least one tenth of everything you earn before spending anything.

lessons.title: Tell Needs Apart From Desires
lessons.key_idea: Your so-called necessary expenses tend to grow to match your income, so you must budget deliberately to live on less than you make.
issues: scene 7: The NEED/DESIRE pill labels on the phone mockup are very small, roughly 16px at 1600 width. That is below the 18px minimum and hard to read. (fix: Raise the pill label font to at least 20px and widen the pills to fit, or shorten the bar lines to make room.)

lessons.title: Put Your Gold to Work
lessons.key_idea: Savings should earn more money for you, as Arkad's did when he lent to a shield maker and reinvested the interest so it kept multiplying.

lessons.title: Guard Your Treasure From Loss
lessons.key_idea: Arkad lost his first savings by trusting a brickmaker to buy jewels, which teaches you to protect your principal and take advice only from people experienced in that field.

lessons.title: Climbing Out of Debt With Determination
lessons.key_idea: Dabasir the camel trader escapes debt by living on seventy percent of his income, paying creditors twenty percent, and saving ten percent.

lessons.title: The Five Laws of Gold
lessons.key_idea: Arkad's son learns that gold comes to those who save it, invest it carefully with wise counsel, and avoid unfamiliar schemes and promises of impossible returns, which ties together every lesson in the book.

plan.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
plan.author: George S. Clason
plan.confidence_note: I know this classic well, including its main parables, characters such as Arkad, Bansir and Dabasir, and its core rules like the Seven Cures and the Five Laws of Gold.
plan.one_liner: Ancient Babylonian parables reveal timeless money rules: save first, spend wisely, and make your gold work.
plan.summary: First published in 1926 as a series of pamphlets, this book teaches personal finance through parables set in ancient Babylon. A chariot builder named Bansir realizes that after years of hard work he has nothing to show for it. He and his friend Kobbi seek out their childhood friend Arkad, now the richest man in the city. Arkad explains that wealth follows simple laws anyone can learn. Keep a part of everything you earn. Live below your income. Put your savings to work, and protect them by taking advice only from people who truly know their trade. Later stories carry these ideas further. A former slave named Dabasir climbs out of debt, and Arkad's son learns the Five Laws of Gold. The message is that steady habits, not luck, build lasting wealth.
